units.title: Groups
units.blurb: Build groups from the Cayley table up: the axioms, the first proofs, the groups ℤₙ and U(n), orders of elements and subgroups.

units.title: Cyclic Groups
units.blurb: Groups made by one element: generators, the orders of powers, and the tidy subgroup structure of ℤₙ.

units.title: Permutation Groups
units.blurb: Rearrangements as a group: composing permutations, cycle notation, orders and signs, and the symmetries of a regular polygon.

units.title: Cosets and Lagrange's Theorem
units.blurb: Cut a group into cosets of a subgroup, prove Lagrange's theorem, and use it to limit the orders of subgroups and elements.

units.title: Normal Subgroups and Homomorphisms
units.blurb: Subgroups you can divide by, maps that respect the operation, and the first isomorphism theorem that ties them together.

units.title: Direct Products and Abelian Groups
units.blurb: Build groups as products, decide when a product is cyclic, and list every finite abelian group of a given order.

units.title: Group Actions and Counting
units.blurb: Let groups move things: orbits and stabilizers, conjugacy classes, Burnside's counting lemma and the Sylow theorems.

units.title: Rings and Ideals
units.blurb: Two operations at once: rings, zero divisors, integral domains and fields, ideals, ring homomorphisms and quotient rings.

units.title: Polynomial Rings
units.blurb: Polynomials with coefficients in a ring or field: division with remainder, gcds, roots and tests for irreducibility.

units.title: Fields and Extensions
units.blurb: Grow fields by adjoining roots: arithmetic in ℚ(√2) and F[x]/(p(x)), minimal polynomials, degrees and the finite fields GF(pⁿ).

topics.title: Binary Operations and Cayley Tables
topics.short: A binary operation combines two elements of a set into one element of the set; a Cayley table lists every product a ∗ b (row a, column b), so you can read off closure, an identity and commutativity.
topics.trouble: Students read b ∗ a when they mean a ∗ b (row first, then column), or take a symmetric table as proof of associativity, which needs every triple.

topics.title: The Group Axioms
topics.short: A group is a set with an associative operation, an identity and an inverse for every element; decide which axiom fails for examples like ℤ under subtraction or ℤₙ under multiplication.
topics.trouble: Students forget to check closure, or count ℤₙ under multiplication as a group although 0 (and every number sharing a factor with n) has no inverse.

topics.title: The Groups ℤₙ and U(n)
topics.short: ℤₙ is {0, 1, …, n − 1} under addition mod n; U(n) is the set of residues coprime to n under multiplication mod n, a group of order φ(n).
topics.trouble: Students put a number sharing a factor with n into U(n), or use addition in U(n) and multiplication in ℤₙ.

topics.title: First Proofs: Uniqueness, Cancellation and Inverses
topics.short: From the axioms alone: the identity and inverses are unique, ab = ac gives b = c, and (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹.
topics.trouble: Students write (ab)⁻¹ = a⁻¹b⁻¹, which holds only when a and b commute, or cancel on opposite sides: ab = ca does not give b = c.

topics.title: The Order of an Element
topics.short: The order of a is the least n ≥ 1 with aⁿ = e (n·a = 0 when the operation is addition), and aᵏ = e exactly when the order of a divides k.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the order of an element with the order of the group, or in ℤₙ multiply a by itself instead of adding it to itself.

topics.title: Subgroups and the Subgroup Test
topics.short: H is a subgroup when it is a group under the same operation; it is enough that H is nonempty and ab⁻¹ ∈ H for all a, b ∈ H (for a finite H, closure alone is enough).
topics.trouble: Students check closure but not inverses for an infinite subset (ℕ is closed under addition but is not a subgroup of ℤ), or forget the identity: the odd integers are not a subgroup.

topics.title: Cyclic Groups and Generators
topics.short: ⟨a⟩ = {aᵏ : k ∈ ℤ} is the smallest subgroup containing a; G is cyclic when one element generates it, and k generates ℤₙ exactly when gcd(k, n) = 1.
topics.trouble: Students think the generators of ℤₙ are the primes below n, or call a group cyclic because it is abelian (U(8) is abelian, but every element squares to 1, so none generates it).

topics.title: Orders of Powers
topics.short: If a has order n, then aᵏ has order n / gcd(n, k); in ℤₙ the element k has order n / gcd(n, k).
topics.trouble: Students divide n by k instead of by gcd(n, k), or miss that k and n − k always have the same order.

topics.title: Subgroups of Cyclic Groups
topics.short: Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic; ℤₙ has exactly one subgroup of each order d dividing n, namely ⟨n/d⟩, and it has φ(d) elements of order d.
topics.trouble: Students list ⟨4⟩ and ⟨8⟩ in ℤ₁₂ as different subgroups, though both are {0, 4, 8}: ⟨k⟩ = ⟨gcd(n, k)⟩.

topics.title: Subgroup Lattices
topics.short: Draw the subgroups of a group ordered by inclusion; for ℤₙ the picture is the divisor diagram of n turned upside down, and you read off intersections and joins.
topics.trouble: Students put ⟨6⟩ above ⟨2⟩ in ℤ₁₂ because 6 > 2; a larger generator gives a smaller subgroup here: ⟨6⟩ ⊂ ⟨2⟩ ⊂ ⟨1⟩ = ℤ₁₂.

topics.title: Permutations and Composition
topics.short: A permutation is a bijection from {1, …, n} to itself; Sₙ is the group of all n! of them under composition, and στ means do τ first, then σ.
topics.trouble: Students compose left to right, but στ applies τ first. Check one input by following it through τ and then through σ.

topics.title: Cycle Notation
topics.short: Follow 1 → σ(1) → σ(σ(1)) → … until you come back, then start a new cycle with the smallest unused number; disjoint cycles commute, and overlapping cycles must be multiplied out.
topics.trouble: Students read a product of overlapping cycles, like (1 2)(2 3), as if the cycles were disjoint, or multiply the cycles left to right.

topics.title: The Order of a Permutation
topics.short: Write σ as disjoint cycles: its order is the lcm of the cycle lengths, and its cycle type tells how many permutations share its shape.
topics.trouble: Students add or multiply the cycle lengths instead of taking their lcm, or take the lcm before rewriting overlapping cycles as disjoint ones.

topics.title: Even and Odd Permutations
topics.short: Every permutation is a product of transpositions, always an even number or always an odd number of them; a k-cycle is even when k is odd, and the even permutations form Aₙ, of order n!/2.
topics.trouble: Students call a 3-cycle odd because 3 is odd; a k-cycle is a product of k − 1 transpositions, so a 3-cycle is even.

topics.title: Dihedral Groups
topics.short: Dₙ is the group of the 2n symmetries of a regular n-gon: rotations rᵏ and reflections rᵏs, with rⁿ = s² = e and sr = r⁻¹s.
topics.trouble: Students assume rs = sr, or that Dₙ has n elements; here Dₙ has 2n elements (some books call it D₂ₙ).

topics.title: Cosets
topics.short: The left coset aH = {ah : h ∈ H}; the left cosets of H all have |H| elements and split G into disjoint pieces, and aH = bH exactly when a⁻¹b ∈ H.
topics.trouble: Students treat cosets as subgroups (only H itself is one), or assume aH = Ha, which holds for every a only when H is normal.

topics.title: Lagrange's Theorem
topics.short: If H is a subgroup of a finite group G, then |H| divides |G|, and the index [G : H] = |G|/|H| counts the cosets.
topics.trouble: Students believe the converse, but a divisor of |G| need not be the order of a subgroup: A₄ has order 12 and no subgroup of order 6.

topics.title: Consequences of Lagrange's Theorem
topics.short: The order of every element divides |G|, so a^|G| = e; a group of prime order is cyclic; and Fermat's and Euler's theorems follow by taking G = U(n).
topics.trouble: Students conclude that a group has an element of every order dividing |G|, but U(8) has order 4 and no element of order 4.

topics.title: Normal Subgroups
topics.short: N is normal when gNg⁻¹ = N for every g, which is the same as gN = Ng; subgroups of abelian groups and subgroups of index 2 are always normal.
topics.trouble: Students think gN = Ng means gn = ng for each n in N, but only the two sets have to match.

topics.title: Quotient Groups
topics.short: When N is normal, the cosets of N form a group G/N with (aN)(bN) = abN, of order |G|/|N|.
topics.trouble: Students take the order of a coset to be the order of its representative: in ℤ₁₂/⟨4⟩ the coset 1 + ⟨4⟩ has order 4, while 1 has order 12 in ℤ₁₂.

topics.title: Group Homomorphisms
topics.short: φ : G → H is a homomorphism when φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b); then φ(e) = e, φ(a⁻¹) = φ(a)⁻¹, and the order of φ(a) divides the order of a.
topics.trouble: Students use the wrong operation on one side (ℤ is added, ℝ* is multiplied), or send a generator of ℤₘ to an element whose order does not divide m.

topics.title: Kernels and Images
topics.short: The kernel {g : φ(g) = e} is a normal subgroup, the image is a subgroup, φ is one-to-one exactly when the kernel is {e}, and |G| = |ker φ| · |im φ|.
topics.trouble: Students collect the elements sent to 0 when the target's identity is 1 (or the reverse), or forget that the kernel always contains e.

topics.title: Isomorphic Groups
topics.short: An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism; to show two groups are not isomorphic, find a property one has and the other lacks: order, being abelian or cyclic, or how many elements have each order.
topics.trouble: Students conclude two groups are isomorphic because they have the same order, or that none exists because one map they tried failed.

topics.title: Cayley's Theorem
topics.short: Every group is isomorphic to a group of permutations: g acts on G by x ↦ gx, so a group of order n sits inside Sₙ.
topics.trouble: Students write the permutation for x ↦ xg instead of x ↦ gx, which reverses products in a nonabelian group.

topics.title: The First Isomorphism Theorem
topics.short: If φ : G → H is a homomorphism, then G/ker φ ≅ im φ; use it to name quotients such as ℤ/nℤ ≅ ℤₙ and Sₙ/Aₙ ≅ ℤ₂.
topics.trouble: Students match G/ker φ with all of H instead of the image of φ, or guess a quotient from its order alone.

topics.title: Direct Products
topics.short: In G × H the operation works coordinate by coordinate; the order of (g, h) is lcm(|g|, |h|), and ℤₘ × ℤₙ ≅ ℤₘₙ exactly when gcd(m, n) = 1.
topics.trouble: Students multiply the orders instead of taking the lcm, or think ℤ₂ × ℤ₂ ≅ ℤ₄ because both have four elements.

topics.title: Classifying Finite Abelian Groups
topics.short: Every finite abelian group is a product of cyclic groups of prime-power order; for order pᵃ the choices match the partitions of a, so you can list them all.
topics.trouble: Students list ℤ₂ × ℤ₄ and ℤ₄ × ℤ₂ as two different groups, or think ℤ₆ and ℤ₂ × ℤ₃ differ (they are isomorphic).

topics.title: Invariant Factors and Telling Abelian Groups Apart
topics.short: Regroup a product of cyclic groups so each order divides the next (ℤ₂ × ℤ₄ × ℤ₃ ≅ ℤ₂ × ℤ₁₂), and count elements of each order to tell abelian groups apart.
topics.trouble: Students merge factors whose orders share a prime, writing ℤ₂ × ℤ₄ as ℤ₈.

topics.title: Group Actions
topics.short: A group acts on a set X when each g moves points, x ↦ g·x, with e·x = x and g·(h·x) = (gh)·x; the orbit of x is everywhere it can go, and its stabilizer is the subgroup that fixes it.
topics.trouble: Students count a point of an orbit twice when two group elements send x to the same place, or assume the stabilizer is always just {e}.

topics.title: The Orbit–Stabilizer Theorem
topics.short: For a finite group, |orbit of x| · |stabilizer of x| = |G|, because the points of the orbit match the cosets of the stabilizer.
topics.trouble: Students multiply when they should divide, or use the size of the whole set X in place of the size of the orbit.

topics.title: Conjugacy Classes and the Class Equation
topics.short: Conjugacy classes are the orbits of G acting on itself by x ↦ gxg⁻¹; in Sₙ they are the cycle types, and |G| = |Z(G)| + the sum of [G : C(x)] over the classes with more than one element.
topics.trouble: Students count the one-element classes of the center again in the sum, or forget that every class size divides |G|.

topics.title: Burnside's Lemma
topics.short: The number of orbits is the average number of points fixed by a group element; count necklaces and colorings up to symmetry by adding up the fixed colorings over the group.
topics.trouble: Students divide the total number of colorings by |G|, which works only when no coloring is fixed by anything except e.

topics.title: The Sylow Theorems
topics.short: If |G| = pᵃm with p not dividing m, then G has subgroups of order pᵃ, they are all conjugate, and their number nₚ divides m and is ≡ 1 (mod p).
topics.trouble: Students use nₚ ∣ |G| instead of nₚ ∣ m, or forget nₚ ≡ 1 (mod p); and nₚ = 1 means the Sylow p-subgroup is normal.

topics.title: Rings
topics.short: A ring is an abelian group under addition with an associative multiplication that distributes over it; ℤ, ℤₙ, matrices and polynomials are rings, and the units are the elements with multiplicative inverses.
topics.trouble: Students assume multiplication commutes or that a ring has a 1: 2ℤ has no identity, and matrix rings are not commutative.

topics.title: Integral Domains and Fields
topics.short: A zero divisor is an a ≠ 0 with ab = 0 for some b ≠ 0; an integral domain has none, every field is one, and ℤₙ is a field exactly when n is prime.
topics.trouble: Students cancel in ℤₙ for composite n, but 2 · 3 = 2 · 0 in ℤ₆ while 3 ≠ 0. Cancellation needs an integral domain.

topics.title: Ideals
topics.short: An ideal is an additive subgroup I with ra and ar in I for every r in R and a in I; nℤ and ⟨d⟩ in ℤₙ are ideals, and every ideal of ℤ has the form nℤ.
topics.trouble: Students check products of two elements of I only; an ideal must absorb products with every element of the ring (ℤ is a subring of ℚ but not an ideal).

topics.title: Ring Homomorphisms
topics.short: φ respects both operations, φ(a + b) = φ(a) + φ(b) and φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b); its kernel is an ideal, and reduction ℤ → ℤₙ and evaluation f ↦ f(c) are the key examples.
topics.trouble: Students check only addition, but x ↦ 2x on ℤ preserves sums and not products.

topics.title: Quotient Rings
topics.short: For an ideal I, the cosets a + I form a ring R/I; compute in ℝ[x]/(x² + 1), where x² can be replaced by −1, and in ℤₚ[x]/(f) by taking remainders.
topics.trouble: Students reduce by the wrong polynomial, or forget to reduce the coefficients mod p as well.

topics.title: Prime and Maximal Ideals
topics.short: P is prime when ab ∈ P forces a ∈ P or b ∈ P, and M is maximal when no ideal lies strictly between M and R; R/P is an integral domain and R/M is a field.
topics.trouble: Students think every prime ideal is maximal, but (x) in ℤ[x] is prime and not maximal, since ℤ[x]/(x) ≅ ℤ is not a field.

topics.title: Polynomial Rings
topics.short: R[x] holds the polynomials with coefficients in R; over an integral domain deg(fg) = deg f + deg g, but in ℤₙ[x] with n composite degrees can drop.
topics.trouble: Students forget to reduce coefficients mod n, or expect deg(fg) = deg f + deg g in ℤ₄[x], where (2x + 1)(2x + 1) = 1.

topics.title: Division and Roots in F[x]
topics.short: Over a field, f = qg + r with deg r < deg g; c is a root of f exactly when x − c divides f, so a nonzero polynomial of degree n has at most n roots.
topics.trouble: Students divide by a leading coefficient as if they were in ℚ instead of multiplying by its inverse mod p, or apply the root bound in ℤₙ[x], where x² − 1 has four roots mod 8.

topics.title: The Euclidean Algorithm for Polynomials
topics.short: Repeated division finds gcd(f, g) in F[x], and running it backward writes the gcd as af + bg, which is how inverses are found in F[x]/(p(x)).
topics.trouble: Students forget to make the gcd monic, or report the last remainder, 0, instead of the one before it.

topics.title: Irreducible Polynomials of Degree 2 and 3
topics.short: A polynomial of degree 2 or 3 over a field is irreducible exactly when it has no root in the field, so over ℤₚ you can test every element.
topics.trouble: Students apply the no-root test to degree 4: x⁴ + 2x² + 1 = (x² + 1)² has no real root but factors.

topics.title: Testing Irreducibility over ℚ
topics.short: Use the rational root test, Gauss's lemma, Eisenstein's criterion (a prime dividing every coefficient but the leading one, with p² not dividing the constant) and reduction mod p.
topics.trouble: Students think a failed Eisenstein test proves a polynomial reducible, or reduce mod a prime that divides the leading coefficient.

topics.title: Field Extensions
topics.short: If p(x) is irreducible over F, then F[x]/(p(x)) is a field containing a root of p; ℚ(√2) = {a + b√2 : a, b ∈ ℚ} is one, with inverses found by the conjugate.
topics.trouble: Students invert a + b√2 term by term, as 1/a + 1/(b√2); multiply by the conjugate a − b√2 instead.

topics.title: Minimal Polynomials and Degree
topics.short: The minimal polynomial of α over F is the monic irreducible polynomial with α as a root, and [F(α) : F] equals its degree.
topics.trouble: Students give a polynomial with root α that factors, such as x⁴ − 4 for √2 instead of x² − 2.

topics.title: Degrees and the Tower Law
topics.short: For fields F ⊆ K ⊆ L, [L : F] = [L : K][K : F]; so [ℚ(√2, √3) : ℚ] = 4, and the cube root of 2 lies in no extension of ℚ whose degree is a power of 2.
topics.trouble: Students add degrees instead of multiplying them, or count [ℚ(√2, √8) : ℚ] as 4 though √8 = 2√2 is already in ℚ(√2).

topics.title: Finite Fields GF(pⁿ)
topics.short: GF(pⁿ) = ℤₚ[x]/(f) for an irreducible f of degree n: add and multiply polynomials mod p and mod f, and find inverses with the Euclidean algorithm.
topics.trouble: Students think GF(4) is ℤ₄ (ℤ₄ is not a field), or forget to reduce by f after multiplying.

topics.title: The Multiplicative Group of a Finite Field
topics.short: The nonzero elements of GF(pⁿ) form a cyclic group of order pⁿ − 1, generated by a primitive element, and GF(pⁿ) contains GF(pᵐ) exactly when m divides n.
topics.trouble: Students assume x is always a primitive element, or that GF(2⁶) contains GF(2⁴) because 4 < 6; it needs 4 ∣ 6.
